cues.text:
Suppose you ask, “How does our order
validator work?”

The name sounds specific to us because
we have the repository open.

Look at the request, though. It contains
neither a function nor a file reference.

The assistant might search if this
session can read the workspace.

Before trusting the explanation, find
the source it actually used.

Look at the return line. A model reads
pieces of this text called tokens.

In this illustration, the space before
quantity travels with the word,
and the operator is another piece.

Tokenizers can split the same line
differently.

That matters when you're estimating how
much source, test output,
and conversation can fit in a request.

Picture the next request after a long
debugging chat.

It can include instructions, parts of
the conversation, selected files,
and tool results.

The client chooses what to include
within a finite budget.

If you need the current condition to be
available, attach the small source file.

Then check whether the answer points
back to that file.

Open order quantity dot pie in the
training repository.

Attach it in Copilot chat and ask what
happens for zero and one.

Read the return expression with me. Zero
is equal to zero, so it passes.

One is greater than zero, so it passes
too. The code explains the observed
behavior.

We still need the issue to decide
whether that behavior is correct.

Add the issue text. The rule now says an
order needs at least one item.

Compare that with the answer we just
traced. The code allows zero because the
comparison includes equality.

The issue requires zero to be rejected.
Ask the assistant to cite both sources

so you can see where each claim came
from.

Try the question twice in two fresh
chats on the same branch.

First attach the issue and the function.
For the second run,
add an unrelated release note.

Read each answer and locate its
evidence. The release note does not
explain this boundary.

Keep the two sources that let a teammate
check the claim quickly.

Now check the explanation against the
original training code.

In an approved runner, call the function
for zero and negative one.

The output shows true for zero and false
for negative one.

That agrees with the comparison you
read.
If the result differs in another run,

compare the checkout and confirm which
version of the function you executed.
